planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall, allowing plenty of root room before summer heat arrives.

directions: This hybrid of Viburnum carlesii and V. macrocephalum produces rounded, snowball-like clusters of pure white florets opening from pale pink buds in mid-spring, carrying a strong, sweet fragrance that surpasses most other viburnums. Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, since a bit of afternoon shade helps flowers last longer in warmer climates. It forms a dense, rounded, multi-stemmed shrub that needs little pruning beyond removing awkward shoots right after flowering, as blooms form on the previous season's wood. Site it near a patio, path, or open window where its perfume can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall so roots establish before extreme heat or cold.

directions: Bred at the U.S. National Arboretum from a cross of Viburnum carlesii and V. macrocephalum, Cayuga is a compact, disease-resistant selection that stays notably tidier and more floriferous than the wilder parent hybrid. Pink buds open in mid-spring into rounded clusters of fragrant white florets that hold up well against powdery mildew and bacterial leaf spot, common problems on other Korean spice-type viburnums. Grow it in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, and prune only lightly right after bloom to maintain its naturally dense, mounded form. Its smaller mature size makes it a good fit for foundation plantings and mixed borders where full-size snowball viburnums would crowd the space.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average garden soil.

directions: This dwarf sport of European cranberrybush forms a tight, rounded mound of dense, deeply lobed, maple-like foliage without producing significant flowers or fruit, making it a foliage and texture plant rather than a bloomer. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates wet soils better than most compact shrubs and colors attractively in fall. Its naturally neat habit needs almost no pruning to stay in bounds, making it a low-maintenance choice for edging a border, anchoring a rock garden, or massing as a low informal hedge. Divide overcrowded plantings or shear lightly in early spring only if a tighter form is desired.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil.

directions: Selected at the U.S. National Arboretum for its exceptionally heavy fruit set, Iroquois bears broad, flat-topped clusters of white spring flowers followed by dense clusters of bright red fruit that ripen earlier and persist longer than the species, drawing songbirds through fall and into winter. Plant in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fruiting is heaviest with a second unrelated dilatatum seedling or cultivar nearby for cross-pollination. Its broad, felted, toothed leaves take on bronze-red fall color before dropping. Prune right after flowering only as needed to maintain shape, since it blooms on the prior year's wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil.

directions: Native to woodlands of Japan and Korea, Wright's viburnum bears flat clusters of white flowers in late spring followed by an especially showy display of glossy, translucent red berries that hang in heavy clusters against the foliage in early fall, ripening well before most other viburnums. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; it tolerates fairly deep shade better than many fruiting viburnums, making it useful under high tree canopy. Its broad, coarsely toothed leaves are largely untroubled by pests and turn a modest burgundy in autumn. Prune lightly right after flowering only to remove crossing or damaged branches, since it needs little shaping to keep an attractive, open, rounded form.
